name: LM27761DSGR
title: LM27761 regulated switched-capacitor inverter, low noise, 2.7 V to 5.5 V in, –1.5 V to –5 V at 250 mA out
summary: The LM27761 makes a regulated negative rail from a positive 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply. A 2 MHz charge pump inverts the input and a negative LDO after it sets the output anywhere from –1.5 V to –5 V with two resistors, delivering up to 250 mA with low noise and ripple. It needs four ceramic capacitors, draws 370 µA running and 7 µA shut down, and has current limit, thermal shutdown and output discharge. It comes in a 2 mm × 2 mm 8-pin WSON with a thermal pad.

circuits.title: Typical application: regulated voltage inverter
circuits.description: A positive 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply on VIN becomes a regulated negative rail on VOUT. C1 is the flying capacitor that the switches swing between the input and the charge-pump output; C3 holds the raw negative voltage at CPOUT, which feeds the internal negative LDO. C2 is the input reservoir and C4 the LDO's output capacitor. R1 from VOUT to VFB and R2 from VFB to ground set the output: VOUT = –1.22 V × (R1 + R2) / R2. EN high runs the part.

charge-pump output; low-ESR ceramic, 10 µF 10 V for higher current
upper divider; 237 kΩ for –1.8 V, 856 kΩ for –3.3 V, 1.54 MΩ for –5 V with R2 = 500 kΩ
lower divider, 50 kΩ or more; 500 kΩ in the characterization circuits

notes: The exposed pad is ground and must be connected (pin 9).

operation.text: A charge pump turns a positive 2.7 V to 5.5 V input into a negative voltage at CPOUT, and a negative low-dropout regulator after it produces the regulated output, adjustable from –1.5 V to –5 V by two resistors. The LDO gives low noise, low ripple, high PSRR and small line and load transients. Four external capacitors are needed for up to 250 mA. Inside are a 2 MHz oscillator, switch drivers and switch array with an input current limit, a reference, a negative bandgap, low-pass filters and the LDO.
A comparator watches VIN. The part shuts down when VIN falls to 2.4 V and runs again once VIN rises above 2.6 V.

Input current is limited, protecting against excess input current and an output shorted to ground; with the output shorted directly to ground the limit is 500 mA typical. Dissipation while limiting is high, and thermal cycling is to be expected.

At light load the pump skips pulses to save quiescent current. The pulse rate has no lower limit and can fall below 2 kHz with no load; it rises with load until the pump runs at its fixed 2 MHz frequency.
In shutdown the output is actively pulled to GND, drawing about 1.85 mA from the output until it gets there.

Shutdown trips at a junction temperature of 150 °C typical and releases at 130 °C typical. Dissipation, and with it self-heating, rises with input voltage and output current. Once self-heating trips the shutdown, the part turns off and on repeatedly and the output pulses; less input voltage, output current or ambient temperature, or better heat removal from the board, ends the cycling.
EN low puts the part in shutdown, where it draws 7 µA and an internal current source of about 1.85 mA pulls its output to ground.
EN above 1.2 V enables the part. Unloaded it draws 370 µA from the input, rising with load. Running, the output sits at the negative of VIN less the drop across the charge pump.

Four large CMOS switches work in two phases. In the first, S1 and S3 close and C1 charges from VIN; in the second, S1 and S3 open, S2 and S4 close and C1 dumps its charge into C3. With C3's positive side at ground, its other side settles at –VIN with no load. Under load the output falls by the switch on-resistance, the capacitor ESR and losses in moving charge between capacitors: the pump behaves like a –VIN source behind the resistance ROUT. A PFM comparator gates the 2 MHz oscillator.
The linear negative regulator after the pump is rated for 250 mA.

Allowed dissipation depends on ambient temperature and on the thermal resistance from junction to air. Equations for PD-MAX and PD together fix the safe combination of voltage drop and continuous current; TA-MAX follows from the 125 °C operating junction limit.
R1 and R2 set VOUT through VOUT = –1.22 V × (R1 + R2) / R2. R2 must be 50 kΩ or more.

All four capacitors should be surface-mount multilayer ceramics, whose ESR is very low (15 mΩ typical or less). Tantalum, OS-CON and aluminium electrolytic capacitors are not recommended because of their higher ESR. X7R and X5R dielectrics are preferred: tolerance as tight as ±10%, and ±15% over –55 °C to +125 °C (X7R) or –55 °C to +85 °C (X5R). Y5V and Z5U are not recommended: tolerance of +80%/–20%, and drift of +22%/–82% from –30 °C to +85 °C (Y5V) or +22%/–56% from 10 °C to 85 °C (Z5U); a 1 µF part of these types can drop to 0.1 µF. Ceramic capacitance also falls with DC bias, raising ripple; keeping the bias well under the rating limits this. The circuit should be tested early with the capacitor chosen for production.

4.7 µF low-ESR ceramic is the usual value; 10 µF 10 V for higher currents. Other values trade ripple against size and cost, and changing it may call for changes to the flying or input capacitor. Too small a C3 lets the ripple grow at the change between PFM and fixed-frequency switching; about 2 µF of effective capacitance prevents the toggling. A 10 µF 10 V capacitor in 0402 has only about 2 µF left at 5 V bias.

C2 supplies charge to the flying capacitor at the start of each charge phase, holding VIN up, and keeps noise off the input that biases the internal analog circuits. Input ripple scales inversely with input capacitance and depends somewhat on VIN, load and flying capacitance. 4.7 µF low-ESR ceramic is usual; near the 250 mA maximum at least 2 µF must remain after DC-bias derating.

C1 moves charge from input to output and sets how much current the output can deliver and how large the ripple is. Too small and the output falls out of regulation at high load; too large and it overwhelms C2 and C3 and ripple grows at input and output. For high-current designs use a low-ESR ceramic of 0.47 µF or 1 µF, rated 10 V. Polarised capacitors must not be used, since C1 can be reverse-biased in operation.
Its value and ESR affect stability, ripple, noise, PSRR and response to transients. A 2.2 µF ceramic placed near VOUT is enough for stability in typical use.
The 2.7 V to 5.5 V source needs good regulation and must be able to deliver the input current. A supply far from the part may need bulk capacitance besides the ceramic bypass.

Because the part switches fast and at high current, layout matters. Put CIN, CCPOUT, C1, COUT, R1 and R2 on the same layer as the part and as close to it as possible, with short, wide traces: CIN to VIN and GND, CCPOUT to its pins and GND, C1 across C1+ and C1–, COUT next to VOUT, R1 and R2 next to VFB. CIN and CCPOUT return to a single point as close to GND as possible. The ground ends of COUT and R2 go back to GND at the thermal pad. Long or narrow traces and vias in these connections add inductance and resistance that hurt transient performance. In the example layout the pins run C1+, C1–, EN, VFB along one side and VIN, GND, CPOUT, VOUT along the other, with C1 over the first pair, R1 and R2 by VFB, CIN by VIN and GND, CCPOUT by CPOUT and COUT by VOUT feeding the load, and the thermal pad tied to the ground plane.
Solder the exposed pad to the board: it carries heat and holds the part mechanically.
